clinician.trajectory_summary: A 34-year-old male farmer from Tchaourou, Borgou region (Lassa-endemic area) presented on 18 January 2018 with a 1-week history of bloody diarrhea (soft, yellowish, mucusy, blood-ribbed stools 3-4 times daily), constant fever, bilious vomiting, odynophagia, intense headaches, and generalized aches. Initial outpatient empiric antimicrobial therapy (paracetamol, quinine, metronidazole, ciprofloxacin, diazepam, albendazole) provided partial improvement for 2 days before symptom recurrence. At hospital admission, vital signs showed fever (39°C), tachycardia (86 bpm), tachypnea (30 cpm), and hypertension (130/100 mmHg). Admission laboratory studies revealed mild thrombocytopenia (platelets 123×10⁹/L), elevated transaminases (ALT 82, AST 62 IU/L), mild renal dysfunction (creatinine 14.13 mg/L), and negative malaria and HIV testing. Initial treatment was empiric for severe sepsis (ceftriaxone, metronidazole, gentamycin, supportive care). On day 3 of hospitalization, hemorrhagic manifestations emerged (melena, facial puffiness, conjunctival hemorrhage), raising clinical suspicion of viral hemorrhagic fever. Detailed history revealed regular rat consumption, consistent with Lassa virus exposure. On day 4 (22 January 2018), the patient was isolated, blood sample was sent to the national laboratory of viral hemorrhagic fever, and specific antiviral therapy was initiated with ribavirin (30 mg/kg IV loading dose followed by 15 mg/kg IV every 6 hours for 4 days), vitamin K1, blood transfusion (two isogroup isorhesius bags), and oxygen therapy. RT-PCR assay confirmed Lassa hemorrhagic fever on 24 January 2018. Despite antiviral therapy, the patient deteriorated and died on 23 January 2018 (day 6 of hospitalization) after repeated convulsions with bradypnea and cardio-circulatory arrest.

On day 4 (22 January 2018), the patient was isolated, blood sample was sent to the national laboratory of viral hemorrhagic fever, and specific antiviral therapy was initiated with ribavirin (30 mg/kg IV loading dose followed by 15 mg/kg IV every 6 hours for 4 days), vitamin K1, blood transfusion (two isogroup isorhesius bags), and oxygen therapy. RT-PCR assay confirmed Lassa hemorrhagic fever on 24 January 2018. Despite antiviral therapy, the patient deteriorated and died on 23 January 2018 (day 6 of hospitalization) after repeated convulsions with bradypnea and cardio-circulatory arrest.

key_supporting_evidence.claim: Patient presented with classic prodromal symptoms of viral hemorrhagic fever: bloody diarrhea, fever, vomiting, headache, and myalgia
Patient resided in Lassa-endemic region (Tchaourou, Borgou) and had documented exposure history (regular rat consumption)
Admission vital signs and physical examination consistent with systemic infection: fever 39°C, tachycardia, tachypnea, hypertension

Laboratory findings at admission showed hematologic and hepatic abnormalities consistent with viral hemorrhagic fever: mild thrombocytopenia (123×10⁹/L), elevated transaminases (ALT 82, AST 62 IU/L), mild renal dysfunction (creatinine 14.13 mg/L)
Hemorrhagic manifestations emerged on day 3 of hospitalization: melena, facial puffiness, and conjunctival hemorrhage, raising clinical suspicion of viral hemorrhagic fever
Blood sample sent to national laboratory of viral hemorrhagic fever on day 4 (22 January 2018) for confirmatory testing
Specific antiviral therapy (ribavirin) initiated on day 4 after hemorrhagic fever suspicion, along with supportive care including blood transfusion and vitamin K1
Lassa hemorrhagic fever confirmed by RT-PCR assay on 24 January 2018
Patient died on day 6 of hospitalization (23 January 2018) despite antiviral therapy, with terminal events of repeated convulsions, bradypnea, and cardio-circulatory arrest

ruled_out_or_less_likely_alternatives.basis: Plasmodium thick drop negative on admission (E003)

Initial empiric antimicrobial therapy (ceftriaxone, metronidazole, gentamycin) did not prevent progression to hemorrhagic manifestations; hemorrhagic phenotype (melena, conjunctival hemorrhage, facial puffiness) on day 3 and confirmed viral etiology by RT-PCR

remaining_uncertainties: Detailed RT-PCR assay methodology, cycle threshold (Ct) value, and viral load quantification (attempted request blocked by validation constraints)
Specific specimen type tested for RT-PCR (blood, serum, or other)
Complete coagulation studies (PT, aPTT, fibrinogen) to fully document hemorrhagic diathesis
Detailed clinical progression from day 4 through day 6: specific organ dysfunction, hemorrhagic manifestations progression, response to ribavirin therapy
